nodeData.note: The first tool of every engineer: measuring in agreed units, checking that equations make sense, and knowing how sure a number is. Own-words notes from OpenStax University Physics Volume 1, chapter 1 (free, CC BY) and Wikipedia; tap a bubble for the page. Worked examples use SI units and g = 9.8 m/s². Search words: SI, metric, prefixes, dimensional analysis, significant figures, uncertainty, conversion.

children.note: A number without a unit says nothing: "the bridge is 40" could be metres or feet. Engineers in Kenya and nearly everywhere use SI, so a drawing from Nairobi reads the same in Mombasa or Mumbai.

children.topic: A quantity is defined by how it is measured
children.note: Length by a rule, time by a clock; speed is then calculated as distance over time. Define it by the method of measuring or by the formula from other measurements.

manas.q: How is a physical quantity defined?

children.topic: Two systems: SI and English units
children.note: SI (metric) is used by almost every country and by all of science. English (imperial) units — feet, pounds, miles — survive mainly in the USA. You will meet inch-based bolts ("SAE") on imported machines.

children.topic: SI is coordinated by the BIPM in Paris
children.note: The International Bureau of Weights and Measures keeps the definitions; since 2019 every base unit is fixed by a constant of nature, not by a metal object.

manas.q: Since 2019, what are SI base units defined by?

children.note: Everything measurable is built from seven base quantities. Learn the unit and its symbol: m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd. Symbols are case-sensitive: "K" is kelvin, "k" is kilo.

manas.q: Name the seven SI base units with their symbols.

children.note: Since 1983: how far light goes through empty space in 1/299 792 458 s. That fixes the speed of light at exactly 299 792 458 m/s — the constant defines the unit.

manas.q: How is the metre defined, and what number does that fix exactly?

children.note: Until 2019 a platinum–iridium cylinder near Paris, which slowly lost about 50 micrograms. Now fixed through the Planck constant and measured on a Kibble balance. The only base unit whose name carries a prefix.

manas.q: What replaced the metal cylinder as the definition of the kilogram?

children.note: Since 1967: the time for 9 192 631 770 vibrations of a caesium atom. GPS and M-Pesa timestamps depend on clocks this exact.

manas.q: What does the second count?

children.note: The base unit for electricity; charge (coulomb) is current × time, so 1 C = 1 A·s.
Thermodynamic temperature; 0 K is absolute zero. A kelvin step equals a Celsius step, and 0 °C = 273.15 K. Write "K", never "°K".

manas.q: Convert 25 °C to kelvin.

children.note: Counts particles (about 6.022 × 10²³ of them). Chemistry and materials courses use it constantly.
Brightness as the eye sees it; used in lighting design. Rare in first-year mechanics.
Multiply or divide base units and you get every other unit. 22 derived units have special names (newton, pascal, joule, watt…); each can still be written in base units.

manas.q: What is a derived unit? Give two examples.

children.note: Length × length and length × length × length. 1 litre is 10⁻³ m³ (a 10 cm cube), one of the non-SI units accepted with SI.

manas.q: How many cubic metres is one litre?

children.note: Distance over time, and change of speed over time. A car at 60 km/h is moving at about 16.7 m/s.
Mass per volume. Water is about 1000 kg/m³, the same as 1 g/cm³: 1000 kg = 10⁶ g spread over 1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³. Steel is about 7850 kg/m³.

manas.q: What is the density of water in kg/m³?

children.note: From F = ma: one newton accelerates one kilogram at one metre per second squared. A 1 kg bag of sugar weighs about 9.8 N on Earth.

manas.q: Write the newton in base units.

children.note: Force spread over an area. Atmospheric pressure is about 101 kPa; a car tyre about 220 kPa above that.
Work = force × distance. Lifting that 1 kg bag by 1 m takes about 9.8 J. 1 kWh of electricity is 3.6 MJ.

manas.q: How many joules in one kilowatt-hour?

children.note: Energy per second. A 2 kW kettle uses 2000 J every second; a 100 W solar panel at full sun gives 100 J each second.
Angle = arc length ÷ radius, so metres cancel. Trig functions in physics formulas expect radians.
Degrees Celsius, litres and electron-volts are allowed but always convertible: °C = K − 273.15, 1 L = 10⁻³ m³, 1 t (tonne) = 1000 kg = 1 Mg.
One unit covers every scale by adding a power-of-ten prefix: nanometres in a chip, kilometres on a road. Memorise the common ones; the full table is on the OpenStax page.

manas.q: What do kilo, mega, giga, milli, micro and nano mean as powers of ten?

children.note: kilo, mega, giga, tera. A 5 GW power station; a 2 TB disk. Capital letters from mega upward.
milli, micro, nano, pico. A 3 mm bolt; a 10 µF capacitor; a 500 nm wavelength.
centi, deci, hecto, deka — common in everyday life (cm, dL, hectare = 100 m × 100 m) but engineers prefer steps of 1000.
No "megagigametre". For mass the prefix goes on the gram, not the kilogram: 1000 kg is 1 Mg (one megagram), also called a tonne.

manas.q: What is 1000 kg written with a single prefix?

children.note: Step 1: kg → g by × 10³, giving 1.93 × 10¹⁶ g. Step 2: the nearest prefixes are peta (10¹⁵) and exa (10¹⁸). Step 3: 10¹⁶ = 10 × 10¹⁵, so 19.3 Pg (petagrams) — a number between 1 and 1000.

manas.q: Express 1.93 × 10¹³ kg using one prefix so the number is between 1 and 1000.

children.note: Also correct, but the convention is a number between 1 and 1000 so the value reads naturally. Both are the same mass.

Multiply by a conversion factor — a fraction equal to one, such as (1 km / 1000 m) — arranged so the unwanted unit cancels. Write the units in every line; if they do not cancel, the fraction is upside down.

manas.q: What is a conversion factor and how do you know which way up to write it?

children.note: Multiply by (1 km per 1000 m): the metres cancel and 80 m becomes 0.080 km. Same answer by prefix: 8.0 × 10¹ m with kilo = 10³ gives 8.0 × 10⁻² km.
60 km/h × (1000 m / 1 km) × (1 h / 3600 s) = 16.7 m/s. Quick rule: divide km/h by 3.6.

manas.q: Convert 90 km/h to m/s.

children.topic: Worked: 10 miles in 20 minutes, in m/s
children.note: First in the given units: half a mile per minute. Then two factors — 1609 m per mile and one minute per 60 s — give 13 m/s. Two factors, two cancellations.
5 L × (10⁻³ m³ / 1 L) = 5 × 10⁻³ m³ = 0.005 m³. Mass of that water ≈ 1000 kg/m³ × 0.005 m³ = 5 kg.

manas.q: A 20-litre jerrycan of water: volume in m³ and mass in kg?

children.topic: Squared and cubed units need the factor twice or thrice
children.note: 1 m² = (100 cm)² = 10 000 cm²; 1 m³ = 10⁶ cm³. Forgetting the power is the classic error in area and volume conversions.

manas.q: How many cm³ in 1 m³?

children.note: A walking speed of 1.4 m/s or a car at 25 m/s is believable; 1400 m/s is not. If the size is wrong by a thousand, a prefix was probably missed.

Every quantity has a dimension built from L (length), M (mass), T (time), I (current), Θ (temperature), N (amount) and J (light). Square brackets mean "dimension of": [v] = LT⁻¹. Dimensions obey algebra like units.

manas.q: What are the seven dimension symbols?

children.note: You can only add, subtract or equate quantities with the same dimension — no apples plus oranges. Both sides of an equation must agree.

manas.q: State the two rules of dimensional consistency.

children.topic: Rule 2: sin, cos, log, exp take pure numbers
children.note: Their arguments must be dimensionless, and their outputs are dimensionless too. sin(at²/s) is fine because LT⁻²·T²/L = 1.
All seven powers zero — a pure number. Angles in radians, ratios, π, 2, efficiency, strain.

children.topic: Worked: πr² or 2πr for the area of a circle?
children.note: [πr²] = 1·L² = L², the dimension of area. [2πr] = L, a length — so it is the circumference. Dimensions pick the right form but not the constant (they cannot tell πr² from 2πr²).

manas.q: Use dimensions to decide which of 4πr² and 4πr³/3 is the volume of a sphere.

children.topic: Worked: is s = vt + ½at² consistent?
children.note: [s] = L. [vt] = LT⁻¹·T = L. [½at²] = LT⁻²·T² = L. All three terms are lengths, so yes. Swap to s = vt² + ½at and the terms become LT and LT⁻¹ — nonsense.

manas.q: Check s = vt² + ½at for dimensional consistency.

children.topic: Uses: catch typos, rebuild forgotten formulas
children.note: A quick dimension check finds algebra slips before the calculator does. It also suggests how a new quantity must depend on others — a tool you will use in fluids (Reynolds number).
Dimensional analysis never finds a dimensionless factor such as ½ or 2π. Those come from the physics.
Measurements are never exact. Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is how closely repeats agree. A reported number should show only the digits you actually know.

manas.q: Explain the difference between accuracy and precision.

children.topic: Accurate vs precise: the GPS target picture
children.note: Dots spread wide but centred on the target: accurate, not precise. Dots tightly grouped but off-centre: precise, not accurate. A good instrument is both.
A length 2.00 m ± 0.02 m means the true value probably lies between 1.98 and 2.02 m. Percent uncertainty = δA/A × 100 % = 1 %.

manas.q: A mass is 5.0 kg ± 0.1 kg. What is the percent uncertainty?

children.topic: Multiplying or dividing: add percent uncertainties
children.note: Area of a 2.00 m ± 1 % by 1.50 m ± 2 % panel: 3.00 m² ± 3 %, i.e. ± 0.09 m².

children.topic: Significant figures: the digits you trust
children.note: 36.7 cm has three; 0.0025 m has two (leading zeros do not count); 1200 is ambiguous — write 1.2 × 10³ or 1.200 × 10³ to say what you mean.

manas.q: How many significant figures in 0.0025 and in 36.70?

children.topic: Multiplication and division: fewest sig figs wins
children.note: 2.3 m × 1.457 m = 3.4 m² (two figures, because 2.3 has only two).

children.topic: Addition and subtraction: fewest decimal places wins
children.note: 12.4 m + 0.057 m = 12.5 m (one decimal place, set by 12.4).

manas.q: 12.4 + 0.057 to the correct number of figures?

children.note: 9.8 m/s² × 5.0 kg = 49 N, not 49.000. Extra digits claim a precision you never measured.
The gap between your result and the accepted value. If it is bigger than your uncertainty, look for a systematic error (a mis-zeroed scale, a stretched tape).
Engineers estimate before they calculate — to size a pump, a budget, a tank — then check the detailed answer against the estimate. Aim for the right power of ten, not the last digit.

children.topic: Method: break it into things you know
children.note: Water for a 50-house estate: 50 houses × 5 people × 100 L/day ≈ 25 000 L/day = 25 m³/day. Each factor is a rough guess; the product is usually within a factor of 2–3.

manas.q: Estimate the daily water need of a 50-house estate and state your assumptions.

children.note: Write the answer as 10ⁿ: 25 m³ is "of order 10 m³". Two estimates that differ by a factor of 3 are the same order of magnitude.

children.topic: Check limits and units at the end
children.note: Does the estimate have the right unit? Does it grow the right way when one input grows? A per-day figure that is far above a river's flow is a sign something is wrong.
The errors first-years make most often — each one has cost marks or, in practice, money.

children.topic: Mixing km/h with m/s in one formula
children.note: Convert everything to base SI before you substitute. v = 60 into s = vt with t in seconds gives nonsense.

children.topic: Forgetting to square the factor for areas
children.note: 1 m² is 10 000 cm², not 100. 1 km² is 10⁶ m².
The kilogram already has a prefix; 1000 kg is 1 Mg or 1 t.

children.topic: Degrees in a trig function expecting radians
children.note: Formulas such as ω = θ/t or arc = rθ need radians. Set the calculator mode before you start.
Round to the significant figures the data allow; keep extra digits only in the middle of a calculation.

children.topic: Writing units in the wrong case
children.note: kg not KG, m not M (M is mega), s not S (S is siemens), K not °K. The symbol is the unit's identity.
Say the answer aloud, then tap the bubble to check against the source page. Five questions, no calculator needed for most.

children.topic: Q1 · Write the pascal and the joule in base units
children.note: Pa = N/m² = kg·m⁻¹·s⁻². J = N·m = kg·m²·s⁻².

manas.q: Write the pascal and the joule in SI base units.
Convert 72 km/h to m/s.

children.topic: Q3 · Is F = mv²/r dimensionally a force?
children.note: [mv²/r] = M·L²T⁻²/L = MLT⁻², the same as [ma]. Yes.

manas.q: Show that mv²/r has the dimensions of force.
Express 0.0000047 m with a metric prefix.

children.topic: Q5 · A tape reads 3.21 m ± 0.01 m. Percent uncertainty?

manas.q: A tape reads 3.21 m ± 0.01 m. What is the percent uncertainty?

children.note: Measure in SI, carry the units through every line, check dimensions before trusting a formula, and report only the digits you know. These four habits catch most engineering errors before they leave the desk.
Next map in this library: Statics — forces, free-body diagrams and equilibrium, where these units (N, N·m) go to work. Medicine and Soil Life libraries use the same SI prefixes.

children.note: Why a bridge, a roof truss or a water-tank stand stays still: the forces and the turning effects on it add to zero. Own-words notes from OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1 (free, CC BY) sections 5.7, 12.1, 12.2; tap a bubble for the page. SI units, g = 9.8 m/s². Search words: statics, equilibrium, free body diagram, FBD, torque, moment, lever arm, reaction, tension, normal force, friction.

maps.title: Statics: forces, free-body diagrams and equilibrium

nodeData.topic: Statics: forces, free-body diagrams and equilibrium
nodeData.note: Why a bridge, a roof truss or a water-tank stand stays still: the forces and the turning effects on it add to zero. Own-words notes from OpenStax University Physics Vol. 1 (free, CC BY) sections 5.7, 12.1, 12.2; tap a bubble for the page. SI units, g = 9.8 m/s². Search words: statics, equilibrium, free body diagram, FBD, torque, moment, lever arm, reaction, tension, normal force, friction.

children.note: Equilibrium for a rigid body: zero linear acceleration and zero angular (turning) acceleration at the same time. At rest in our frame it is in static equilibrium; moving at constant velocity it is in dynamic equilibrium — the same equations apply.

manas.q: Define equilibrium of a rigid body.

children.note: A particle has no size, so only forces matter. A rigid body has size, so where a force acts matters too — that is what adds torque to the problem.
A crate at rest on a moving lorry is in static equilibrium for the driver and dynamic equilibrium for someone on the road. The laws are the same in every inertial frame.

children.topic: Newton's first law is the statics law
children.note: No net force → no change in motion. Statics is Newton's first law applied to forces and to torques.

manas.q: Which of Newton's laws does statics rest on?

children.note: Six forces cover most first-year problems. Each has a fixed direction rule — learn the rule and the diagram draws itself.

manas.q: List the common forces and the direction each one acts in.

children.note: Acts at the centre of mass. A 20 kg beam weighs 20 × 9.8 = 196 N. The only common force that needs no contact.

manas.q: What is the weight of a 60 kg person on Earth?

children.topic: Normal force N, perpendicular to the surface
children.note: The push of a surface on the body, always at right angles to the surface and away from it. On a slope it is tilted, not vertical.

children.topic: Tension T, along the rope, away from the body
children.note: A rope can only pull. The same tension acts at both ends of a light rope.

children.topic: Friction f, along the surface, opposing motion
children.note: Opposes the motion or the intended motion. Static friction can be anything up to a maximum μₛN; kinetic friction is μₖN.

manas.q: In which direction does friction act on a block held still on a slope?

children.note: A hand, a cable from a winch, a wind load — drawn at the angle the problem states.

children.topic: Spring force, towards the natural length
children.note: Proportional to the stretch or compression (Hooke's law). Pushes or pulls back towards the unstretched position.
What a support can push back with depends on how it is made. Count the unknowns a support brings before you count equations.

manas.q: How many unknowns do a roller, a pin and a fixed support each add?

children.note: One force perpendicular to the surface. It cannot pull or resist sliding.
A force of unknown size and direction — write it as two components. It cannot resist turning.
Two force components plus a moment, because the wall stops the beam turning. A cantilever balcony is this case.
Draw the body alone, with every external force on it as an arrow. Done right, the diagram is most of the solution; done wrong, no algebra can save it.

manas.q: State the four rules for a free-body diagram.

children.note: Sketch the object (a dot if treating it as a particle) with x–y axes. Circle it so you only mark forces acting ON it.

children.topic: Rule 2: all external forces, no net force
children.note: Weight, normal, tension, friction, applied, spring. Never draw the net force; never draw forces the body exerts on other things; never both halves of an action–reaction pair.

manas.q: Name two things that must never appear on a free-body diagram.

children.topic: Rule 3: replace angled forces by components
children.note: Draw the x and y components and put a squiggle through the original arrow so you do not count it twice.
Two blocks, two diagrams. Forces between them appear on both, equal and opposite.
If the body accelerates, note the acceleration beside the diagram in another colour, not as an arrow on it.
Forces: pull P at 30° above the ground, weight down, normal up, friction backwards. Components of P: P cos 30° forward, P sin 30° upward — the upward part reduces the normal force.

manas.q: A sled is pulled by 100 N at 30°. Forward and upward components?

children.note: Forward 100 × cos 30° = 86.6 N; upward 100 × sin 30° = 50 N. Check: 86.6² + 50² ≈ 100².

children.topic: Example: two blocks on an incline
children.note: Block A on top of block B on a slope: separate diagrams. Friction from B on A points one way; friction from A on B the opposite way — they are a third-law pair, equal in size.
Ask: which way would the body slide if the surface were ice? Friction points the other way.

children.topic: First condition: forces sum to zero
children.note: ΣF = 0, which in components means ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0 (and ΣFz = 0 in 3-D). This alone solves particle problems — knots, hanging loads, blocks held on slopes.

manas.q: Write the first equilibrium condition in component form.

children.topic: Worked: lamp on two symmetric cables
children.note: A 5.0 kg lamp (49 N) hangs from two cables, each 30° above horizontal. Vertical: 2T sin 30° = 49, so T = 49 N. Horizontal: the two T cos 30° cancel by symmetry.

manas.q: A 5 kg lamp hangs from two cables at 30° above horizontal. Tension in each?

children.note: At 10° above horizontal: T = 49 / (2 sin 10°) = 141 N — nearly three times the lamp's weight. A perfectly horizontal cable would need infinite tension, which is why washing lines sag.

manas.q: Why can a clothes line never be pulled perfectly straight?

children.topic: Worked: block held on a 30° slope
children.note: 10 kg block at rest on a 30° incline. Along the slope: friction f = mg sin 30° = 98 × 0.5 = 49 N, up the slope. Perpendicular: N = mg cos 30° = 84.9 N.

manas.q: A 10 kg block rests on a 30° slope: find the friction and normal force.

children.note: μ must be at least f/N = 49/84.9 = 0.58 = tan 30°. In general a block stays put while tan θ ≤ μₛ.

children.topic: Choose axes to suit the problem
children.note: On a slope, take x along the slope and y perpendicular to it; then N has no x-component and only weight needs splitting.
Στ = 0: the turning effects about any axis also cancel. Needed whenever the body has size — beams, ladders, seesaws, cranes, bridge decks.

manas.q: Write the second equilibrium condition and say when it is needed.

children.note: τ = r F sin θ: the force times the perpendicular distance from the pivot to its line of action. Unit N·m (not joules, though the base units match).

manas.q: A 200 N force acts 1.5 m from a hinge at right angles. Torque?

children.note: Pick one sense as positive and keep it. Many textbooks and this library use anticlockwise = +.

children.topic: A force through the pivot has zero torque
children.note: Its lever arm is zero. This is the trick for choosing the pivot: put it where an unknown force acts, and that unknown disappears from the torque equation.

manas.q: Where should you put the pivot to make an unknown force vanish from the torque equation?

children.note: If forces sum to zero and torques about one point sum to zero, then torques about every other point sum to zero too — shifting the pivot adds R × ΣF, which is zero. So you choose the pivot for convenience.

manas.q: Why are we free to choose any pivot point in an equilibrium problem?

children.note: With the z-axis as the rotation axis the six equations shrink to ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, Στz = 0. Three unknowns at most can be found; more unknowns means the problem is statically indeterminate.

manas.q: How many independent equilibrium equations does a planar problem give?

children.topic: Centre of mass carries the weight
children.note: For torque purposes, a uniform beam's whole weight acts at its midpoint; a uniform plate's at its centre.
Find the centre of mass first (given, or by balancing). A loaded lorry or a crane with its boom out has it well away from the geometric middle.
OpenStax's problem-solving strategy for rigid bodies in equilibrium. Follow it in order every time; most mistakes come from skipping step 2.

manas.q: List the five steps for solving a static-equilibrium problem.

children.topic: 1 · Identify the body, the forces, the question
children.note: Which object? What acts on it? What is asked, and what is given — including facts hidden in the wording ("uniform beam" means weight at the centre).

children.topic: 2 · Draw the free-body diagram and pick a pivot
children.note: Axes, every force, components, labels. For an unknown force guess a direction; a negative answer later means it points the other way. Mark the pivot and the lever arms.

manas.q: What does a negative answer for an unknown force mean?

children.note: ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, Στ = 0 about the chosen pivot, each force with its sign.
As many equations as unknowns. Keep symbols until the end; substitute numbers last.
Right unit (N or N·m)? Sensible size? Re-solve about a different pivot as an independent check.
Three problems, each recomputed step by step. Cover the answer and try first.

children.topic: A · Seesaw: where must the heavier child sit?
children.note: A 30 kg child sits 2.0 m left of the pivot. A 40 kg child sits on the right at distance d. Torques about the pivot: 30 × 9.8 × 2.0 = 40 × 9.8 × d, so d = 60/40 = 1.5 m. (g cancels.)

manas.q: 30 kg at 2.0 m balances 40 kg at what distance?

children.note: ΣFy = 0: the pivot pushes up with (30 + 40) × 9.8 = 686 N.

children.topic: B · Beam on two supports with a load
children.note: Uniform beam, 4.0 m, 20 kg (196 N at its middle, 2.0 m from A). A 60 kg load (588 N) sits 1.0 m from support A. Find the support reactions R_A and R_B.

manas.q: Set up the torque equation about A for the beam example.

children.note: R_B × 4.0 = 196 × 2.0 + 588 × 1.0 = 392 + 588 = 980 N·m, so R_B = 245 N. R_A drops out because it acts at A.
R_A + R_B = 196 + 588 = 784 N, so R_A = 784 − 245 = 539 N. The support nearer the load carries more — as expected.

manas.q: In the beam example, why does R_A carry more than R_B?

children.note: R_A × 4.0 = 196 × 2.0 + 588 × 3.0 = 392 + 1764 = 2156 N·m, so R_A = 539 N. Same answer from a different pivot: solved.
A 1000 L tank (1000 kg of water, 9800 N) plus a 200 kg tank-and-frame (1960 N) stands on four equal legs. Symmetry: each leg carries 11 760 / 4 = 2940 N. Each leg's footing must take about 3 kN.

manas.q: A full 1000 L tank on a 200 kg stand with four legs: load per leg?

children.note: Symmetry breaks; use torques about one pair of legs to find how the load shifts — the legs under the heavy side carry more. This is why stands are levelled.
Each of these has been seen in first-year scripts — and in collapsed sheds.

children.topic: Drawing the net force or "ma" as a force
children.note: Only real pushes and pulls go on the diagram.

children.topic: Normal force drawn vertical on a slope
children.note: It is perpendicular to the surface, so it tilts with the slope.

children.topic: Both halves of an action–reaction pair on one body
children.note: They act on different bodies; only one belongs on any single diagram.

children.topic: Using the full distance instead of the lever arm

children.topic: Q5 · Is a car cruising at constant 80 km/h in equilibrium?
children.note: Yes — dynamic equilibrium: no acceleration, forces and torques balance.

manas.q: Is a car at a steady 80 km/h on a straight road in equilibrium?
